title: Arrow prayers (Nehemiah 2:4)
hook: before the king answers, Nehemiah fires a silent prayer upward

segments.voice: Yesterday, the examen: Ignatius's nightly look back over the day. Your line was where was he today? Did you find a moment, or a miss? Today, a prayer that takes about one second. Day one hundred three.

You know the moment. Someone important turns to you and says, so, what do you want? The interview. The doctor. The boss with one minute between meetings. Your mouth is open, and there's no time to think. Now go to the Persian court, about four and a half centuries before Jesus. A Jewish man named Nehemiah is cupbearer to King Artaxerxes: he pours the king's wine and tastes it first. He's just heard that the walls of Jerusalem are rubble, and he can't hide his grief. The king notices his sad face, and the text says, "Then I was very sore afraid." A sad servant in front of a king was a risk. And then the king asks the question. What do you want? Nehemiah has maybe a second. Today is what he does with it.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU WANT?` → `A CUPBEARER TO A KING.` → `ONE SECOND TO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the King James Bible: "Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven." And in the very next breath, he answers the king. That's it. No words recorded, no kneeling, no closed eyes. Between the question and the answer, a prayer went up, and nobody in the room saw it. Christians came to call this kind of prayer an arrow prayer: short, silent, fired upward in the middle of life. Old writers told of monks in the Egyptian desert who prayed this way all day, in quick, brief bursts. But notice something about Nehemiah. The arrow didn't come from nowhere. In chapter one, when the bad news first came, he sat down and wept, and fasted and prayed for days. Months passed before the king ever asked. So the arrow flew from a bow that had been strung for a long time. The long prayer and the short one belong together. The Bible is full of these arrows. A mother pleading for her daughter, in Matthew: "Lord, help me." Peter, sinking into the waves: "Lord, save me." Three words each. And Paul tells the church in Thessalonica, "Pray without ceasing," which many Christians hear not as a command to never stop talking, but as an invitation to keep a door open all day. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants all have their short prayers for the middle of things. For Nehemiah, it worked: the king said yes, and he went home to rebuild the wall.
screen: `A PRAYER BETWEEN QUESTION AND ANSWER.` · `THE BOW WAS STRUNG FOR MONTHS.` · `LORD, HELP ME. LORD, SAVE ME.` · then, large: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse the arrow. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next conversation you'll have today. Who is it with? A coworker, a child, a cashier, someone on the phone. Picture their face. Now, before the first word, take three seconds. If you pray, you can send up a short line, like the mother's, "Lord, help me," or a few words of your own. If you don't, take one slow breath and wish them well. Then let the rest of the time be quiet. When that conversation actually comes, do it for real. Three seconds. The bell holds the time.
Arrow prayers. Short, silent prayers sent up in the middle of life, like Nehemiah's before the king. Today's word.
Your line: short prayers fly. Today, before your next hard conversation, take three seconds first. Nobody has to know. Day one hundred three.

screen: `DAY 103 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PRAYING FOR OTHERS BY NAME.`

howItsDone: Many Christians pray short, silent prayers through the day, before a meeting, at a siren, in a moment of fear, alongside longer times of prayer; Orthodox Christians often use the Jesus Prayer this way.

it only says he prayed to the God of heaven. the words aren't recorded.
Nehemiah had already been praying about this for a long time
in chapter one he wept, fasted and prayed for days. the king's question came months later.
short prayers belong to only one church

fork.setup: you're Nehemiah. the king has seen your sad face and asks what you want. you have about one second. what do you do?
options: answer at once with the whole plan.
fork.reveal: "So I prayed to the God of heaven." then he answered. the king said yes, and Nehemiah went home to rebuild Jerusalem's walls.

original.note: Hebrew: prayer. the verb in Nehemiah 2:4, "I prayed," comes from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer needs time, a quiet room and closed eyes.
what it means: Nehemiah prays in the one second between a king's question and his answer, and nobody sees it.
what a scholar hears: a cupbearer tasted and served the Persian king's wine, a trusted post; a servant looking sad before the king was a real risk, which is why he was afraid.

sources.ref: Augustine, Letter 130 (to Proba), on the brief prayers of the Egyptian monks

notes: Date: Nehemiah's request to Artaxerxes (I) is usually placed around 445 BCE, 'about four and a half centuries before Jesus'. Confirm.
'Months passed': Nehemiah 1:1 is in Chisleu and 2:1 in Nisan, roughly four months apart. Confirm.
Cupbearer tasting the king's wine first is a common description of the office; the text itself only says he was the king's cupbearer (1:11) and served wine (2:1). Confirm the phrasing.
'Arrow prayer' as a Christian term and the link to the Egyptian desert monks follows Augustine's Letter 130, which describes brief prayers 'darted' quickly; paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm.
Reading of 'Pray without ceasing' as keeping a door open all day is presented as how many Christians hear it; confirm it is fair across traditions.
